name: Ready-to-Resume Plan
summary: A short note written just before an interruption that records where a task stands and what the next step is, so the mind can let go of it.
explanation:
A ready-to-resume plan is a brief written plan that you make when you must leave a task before it is finished. It captures three things: where you are, what is still open, and the exact next step you will take when you come back.

The idea comes from Sophie Leroy and Theresa Glomb (2018). They studied what happens when people are interrupted and expect time pressure when they return to the interrupted task. Those people kept thinking about the unfinished task, showed more attention residue, and performed worse on the interrupting task. When participants spent about a minute writing a ready-to-resume plan before switching, attention residue dropped and performance on the interrupting task improved.

Why it works: an unfinished task keeps pulling at attention because the mind does not trust that it will be picked up again (see the Zeigarnik effect and open loops). Writing down the next step gives the mind that guarantee, which is the same mechanism behind the plan-making effect. It also shortens the resumption lag later, because the context you need is already on paper.

How to apply it: before you answer the call, join the meeting, or end the day, write two or three lines in the task, a scratch file, or a top of mind note. Use the format "I am at X. Next: Y. Watch out for Z." Keep it short so that the habit stays cheap enough to do every time. Hemingway's habit of stopping mid-sentence (the Hemingway bridge) and a daily shutdown ritual are close cousins of the same practice.

articles.title: Tasks Interrupted: How Anticipating Time Pressure on Resumption of an Interrupted Task Causes Attention Residue and Low Performance on Interrupting Tasks and How a "Ready-to-Resume" Plan Mitigates the Effects
